Group 6 - Acute coronary syndrome and Africa

Studio wall

Author

Myself, Rachana, Jayani (Panels A & B); Myself, Madhumitha, Jai, Jayani (Panel C); Myself, Anmol, Charitha (Panel E)

Spine

Who arrives in acute coronary crisis, which habits travel with that crisis, and where in Africa is life short?

This sentence stays at the top. Every panel must attach to it. If a plot cannot be introduced in a clause that hangs off this line, it is off the wall.

Introduction - the tables we own

This folder is ours for the ten days. Four tables, four shapes.

  • Panel A (panel-A.csv) - ACS clinic file: age, height, weight, BMI, ejection fraction, lipids. sex and obesity for grouping.
  • Panel B (panel-B.csv) - same people, categorical information.
  • Panel C (panel-C.csv) - Africa data.
  • Panel D (panel-D.csv) - selected Hinkley monitoring well chromium data.

We load from this folder:

2. Ask

Questions this table can answer. 1. Is age associated with EF? 2. Is TC associated with LDLC? 3. Does EF differ between males and females? 4. Does obesity status vary between males and females? 5. Is obesity independent of age? 6. Does height, age and sex of the person effect BMI? 7. Does EF decrease with age? 8. Does the proportion of obese and non obese patients differ between males and females? 9. Do obese patients generally show higher BMI values than non-obese patients? 10.How many obese and non-obese participants are there in the dataset? 11.How are the participants’ weights distributed? 12.What is the age distribution of the participants?

One question this table cannot answer. 1. Is regular physical activity associated with ejection fraction (EF)? 2. Does smoking cause higher cholesterol? 3. Do diabetic patients have higher BMI? 4. Does high blood pressure lead to lower EF? 5. Does obesity cause a lower ejection fraction? 6. Which patients had a STEMI, NSTEMI, or Unstable Angina? 7. Will patients with high BMI develop heart disease in the future?

3. Choose a mark

Use bar charts, histograms, box plots, or scatter plots depending on the type of variables and the questions being answered.

4. Predict

I expect some variables such as BMI and obesity status to show clear differences, while relationships involving age, EF.

5. Make

Create the graphs using ggplot2, and summaries or statistical tests where appropriate to examine the pattern in the data.

  1. Is age associated with EF?

  ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      x = age,
      y = EF
    )
  )

6. Say

  1. Does height, age and sex of the person effect BMI? Ans. This graph is special because height and BMI are shown through position, while sex is shown by color and age by the size of the points.

7. Limit

Panel A can only answer questions using the variables available in the table. It cannot answer questions about smoking, diagnosis, diabetes etc..

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. 1.Does smoking status vary by sex? 2.Are the observed obesity patterns for males and females different from what would be expected by chance? 3.Does smoking status differ across STEMI, NSTEMI, and Unstable Angina patients? 4.Is obesity distributed differently across the different diagnosis groups? 5.Is cardiogenic shock more common in certain diagnosis groups? 6.Does the type of entry, Radial or Femoral, differ across diagnosis groups? 7.Is diabetes associated with high blood pressure? 8.Is cardiogenic shock associated with smoking status?

One question this table cannot answer. 1. What is the average age of patients with STEMI? Ans. Age is not available in Panel B.

  1. Do obese patients have a higher BMI than non-obese patients? Ans. BMI values are not available in Panel B.

  2. Do smokers have higher cholesterol levels than non-smokers? Ans. Cholestrol levels are not available in Panel B.

  3. Do patients with diabetes have a lower ejection fraction? Ans. Ejection fraction is not available in Panel B.

  4. Which patients recovered faster after treatment? Ans. Panel B does not contain treatment or recovery time information.

  5. How long had each patient been smoking? Ans. Panel B gives smoking status but not the duration of smoking.

3. Choose a mark

Use bar chart and mosaic plots to compare qualitative variables, followed by chi-square test.

4. Predict

I expect some qualitative variables to show clear differences between groups, while others may show little or no difference.

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. 1. Which countries have the lowest life expectancy? 2. Is there a relation between population of a country and GDP per capita? Is GDP per capita higher with higher population?

One question this table cannot answer.

  1. Why do some countries have a high GDP per capita but low life expectancy?
  2. What percentage of women help a country build its GDP per capita?

3. Choose a mark

Question 1: Which countries have the lowest life expectancy?

Mark: A map of Africa where countries are filled based on life expectancy.

Question 2: Is there a relation between population of a country and GDP per capita? Is GDP per capita higher with higher population?

Mark:A map of Africa showing GDP per capita using fill colour and population using border colour.

4. Predict

We expect life expectancy to vary across African countries. We also expect population and GDP per capita to show some relationship, but it may not be very strong.

5. Make

C_modd |>
  ggformula::gf_sf(
    geometry = ~geometry,
    fill = ~lifeExp,
    color = "black"
  )
C_modd |>
  ggformula::gf_sf(
    geometry = ~geometry,
    fill = ~gdpPercap,
    color = ~pop
  ) |>
  ggformula::gf_refine(
    ggplot2::scale_color_gradient(
      low = "#A1FA4F",
      high = "#183E0C"
    )
  ) |>
  ggformula::gf_refine(
    ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(
      low = "#FFFE91",
      high = "#BA1B1B"
    )
  )

6. Say

Title: Africa: A Data Visualization

Caption: These maps show differences in life expectancy, population and GDP per capita across African countries.

One statement we will stand by: The data shows clear differences in life expectancy, population and GDP per capita across African countries

7. Limit

This panel only contains data from 2007, so we cannot study how these values changed over time. It also does not contain gender data, so we cannot compare life expectancy or GDP per capita between women and men.

    names_to = "chromium_type",
    values_to = "concentration"
  )

  D_long,
  ggplot2::aes(
    x = well,
    y = concentration,
    fill = chromium_type
  )
) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(position = "dodge")

6. Say

Title: Chromium levels across selected Hinkley monitoring wells

Caption: These graphs compare Cr(VI) and total dissolved chromium, Cr(T), across seven selected monitoring wells from the Second Quarter 2026 Hinkley plume map.

One statement we will stand by: Chromium concentrations differ across the selected wells, and Cr(T) is equal to or slightly higher than Cr(VI) at most of the wells.

7. Limit

This panel uses only seven selected monitoring wells from one part of the Second Quarter 2026 plume map. It does not represent every well in Hinkley, and it cannot explain why chromium levels differ between wells or what health effects they may have caused.

Panel E — Hunches

Setting up

The libraries are already loaded above this section. The code below assumes the six datasets have already been loaded as hunch_1 through hunch_6.

Hunch 1 — Friends vs House vs Modern Family

Prepare the data

hunch_1 <- hunch_1 |>
  janitor::clean_names()

names(hunch_1)
[1] "students"      "friends"       "house"         "modern_family"

The ratings are stored as text such as 7/10. Convert them to numbers, then put the three shows into one column so their ratings can be compared.

hunch_1_mod <- hunch_1 |>
  mutate(
    friends = readr::parse_number(friends),
    house = readr::parse_number(house),
    modern_family = readr::parse_number(modern_family)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(friends, house, modern_family),
    names_to = "show",
    values_to = "scores"
  )

A case is one student who was asked to rate the TV shows. The students column is an identifier for each respondent. The ratings for Friends, House, and Modern Family are quantitative variables because the students rated the shows out of 10. Missing values mean a respondent did not provide a rating for that show.

2. Ask

Q1. How do the ratings differ between Friends, House, and Modern Family when each pair of shows is compared?

3. Choose a mark

I will use a bar chart to compare the average ratings of the three TV shows. The x-axis will represent the shows, and the y-axis will represent their average ratings. An ANOVA test will help determine whether the mean ratings differ statistically.

4. Predict

I predict that the average ratings will differ between the three shows, with one show receiving a higher average rating than the others.

5. Make

hunch_1_mean |>
  gf_col(
    mean_score ~ show,
    fill = ~ show
  ) |>
  gf_refine(
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c(
        "friends" = "yellow",
        "house" = "lightblue",
        "modern_family" = "pink"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  gf_labs(
    title = "Which TV Show Received the Highest Rating?",
    subtitle = "Average ratings of Friends, House, and Modern Family",
    x = "TV Show",
    y = "Average Rating (out of 10)",
    fill = "TV Show",
    caption = "Source: FOSEDA Panel E, Hunch 1 dataset"
  ) |>
  gf_theme(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

6. Say

The bar chart compares the average ratings of the three shows.

Finding to report: The show with the highest average rating is , while the show with the lowest average rating is . The ANOVA result indicates whether the differences between the mean ratings are statistically significant. Fill in these blanks after checking the graph and ANOVA output.

7. Limit

The ratings represent only the respondents in this dataset. They cannot establish which show is most popular among the general population. Missing ratings may affect the comparison because some respondents may not have watched every show. The data also cannot explain why respondents prefer one show over another.

    y = "Number of Respondents",
    fill = "Belief in AI",
    caption = "Source: FOSEDA Panel E, Hunch 4 dataset"
  ) |>
  gf_theme(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

6. Say

The graph compares Yes and No responses across genders in the Art and Design programs.

Finding to report: The distribution of AI belief appears ___ between male and female respondents in Art, while the pattern in Design appears . This suggests that the relationship between gender and AI belief across the two programs. Fill in the blanks after checking the graph.

7. Limit

The data records the respondents’ beliefs but does not explain why those beliefs exist. It cannot establish that gender or academic program causes a particular belief. The findings may not represent all art and design students.

2. Ask

Q1. How does having tattoos relate to people’s opinions about tattoo attractiveness, and how do these opinions differ by gender?

3. Choose a mark

I will use bar charts separated by gender to compare Yes and No opinions about tattoo attractiveness. The x-axis will represent the opinions, and the y-axis will show the number of respondents.

For the simplified graph, the bar colors will represent the opinions rather than tattoo ownership. This makes the comparison between Yes and No responses within each gender easier to read. Because this graph does not use Has_tattoos?, it only answers the part of the question about opinions by gender.

4. Predict

I predict that most respondents may consider tattoos attractive, but opinions may differ between male and female respondents.

7. Limit

The data records opinions about tattoo attractiveness, not objective attractiveness. It cannot establish whether tattoos actually make someone more attractive or explain why respondents hold particular opinions. The simplified graph also does not show whether respondents have tattoos themselves, so it cannot establish whether tattoo ownership is related to those opinions.

8. Conclusion

Conclusion

Through Panels A to E, we worked with different kinds of data and tried to understand what patterns we could find from them.

Panels A and B were mainly related to health data. Panel C was about African countries and included life expectancy, population and GDP per capita. Panel D was about chromium levels in selected monitoring wells in Hinkley.

Panel E was different because it included six different hunches. In these hunches, we explored topics like TV show ratings, personality types, allowance, belief in AI among Art and Design students, making friends and opinions about tattoos and attractiveness.

From all these panels, I understood that different types of data need different ways of analysing and visualising them. We also had to be careful not to say that one variable causes another just because we found a difference or relationship.

There were also limitations in each panel. Some datasets had missing values, some had only a limited number of responses, and the data we collected cannot represent everyone.

Overall, this project helped me understand how to look at a dataset, ask questions from it, choose a suitable graph or test and then explain what the result actually means.
